L0@P0: The Stock-Bond Correlation: A Tale of Two Days
L1@P0: in the U.S. Treasury Bond Market
L2@P0: Grace Xing Hu, Zhao Jin, and Jun Pan*
L3@P0: First Draft: February 3, 2023
L4@P0: This Draft: December 28, 2024
L5@P0: Abstract
L6@P0: Motivated by the central importance of U.S. Treasury (UST) and the increasing concern
L7@P0: over its resilience, we construct a high-frequency measure of stock-bond correlation to
L8@P0: capture UST safety, and more importantly, its riskiness. On days with highly negative
L9@P0: stock-bond correlations, safety matters the most and the pricing of global assets is
L10@P0: determined by their relative safety. For UST, the premier safe asset, the demand
L11@P0: for safety widens its convenience yield, shrinks the term premium, and breaks the
L12@P0: transmission from UST to USD. By contrast, on days with high stock-bond correlations,
L13@P0: UST pauses its safety status and becomes a source of risk, with increased volatility
L14@P0: and higher term premium. Prominent bond risky days captured by sudden and large
L15@P0: increases of our stock-bond measure are FOMC announcements (interest-rate risk),
L16@P0: 2020 dash for cash (dealer-capacity risk), and 2021 inflation surge. Overall, our measure
L17@P0: is unique in capturing the dual and contrasting roles of UST – sounding the alarm when
L18@P0: UST shifts abruptly from safety to risky.
L19@P0: Keywords: Flights-to-safety, stock-bond correlation, UST resilience, Treasury convenience
L20@P0: JEL Classification: G12, G15
L21@P0: *Hu (hux@pbcsf.tsinghua.edu.cn) is from PBC School of Finance at Tsinghua University. Jin
L22@P0: (zhaojin@cufe.edu.cn) is from School of Finance at Central University of Finance and Economics. Pan
L23@P0: (junpan@saif.sjtu.edu.cn) is from Shanghai Advanced Institute of Finance at Shanghai Jiao Tong University. We benefited from extensive discussions with Darrell Duffie and valuable comments from Paul Calluzzo
L24@P0: (discussant), Wenxin Du (discussant), Erica Li (discussant) and Jun Liu and the seminar participants at
L25@P0: 2023 Summer Institute of Finance Conference, 2023 Financial Management Association Annual Meeting,
L26@P0: 2024 Asian Finance Association, 2024 China International Conference of Finance, and 2024 Northern Finance Association Annual Conference. The paper was previously circulated under the title “Comovements
L27@P0-1: in Global Markets and the Role of U.S. Treasury”.1. Introduction
L28@P1: The U.S. Treasury bond market is widely regarded as the world’s deepest and most important market. The pricing of U.S. Treasury bonds establishes the benchmark yield curve
L29@P1: for borrowing costs across different horizons and facilitates the price discovery of monetary
L30@P1: policies, inflation risk, and other macroeconomic fundamentals. Beyond serving as a key
L31@P1: economic indicator, the U.S. Treasury market carries significant political importance. It is
L32@P1: critical in financing the U.S. government’s expanding deficits, and attracts large foreign holdings because of the dollar’s role as the primary reserve currency. Overall, a well-functioning
L33@P1: U.S. Treasury market is important for the global economy and essential for the U.S.
L34@P1: In this paper, we examine the dual and contrasting roles of the U.S. Treasury bond
L35@P1: market – both as a destination of safety and a source of risk. The safety nature of the
L36@P1: U.S. Treasury has been well established in the literature, via episodes of flights-to-safety
L37@P1: (Baele, Bekaert, Inghelbrecht, and Wei 2019) and the global safety demand for U.S. Treasury
L38@P1: (Jiang, Krishnamurthy, and Lustig 2021). Contrary to its safe-asset role, however, the U.S.
L39@P1: Treasury market can also, at times, poses substantial risks, as illustrated by the 2020 dash
L40@P1: for cash. This is especially true when the U.S. Treasury market is mired in concerns over
L41@P1: surging inflation, monetary policy uncertainty, or dealer-capacity risk. Indeed, while its
L42@P1: status as a primary safe haven asset remains well-established, growing concerns about the
L43@P1: resilience of the U.S. Treasury market and the sustainability of U.S. government debt have
L44@P1: intensified in recent years (Duffie 2023; Duffie et al. 2023). These challenges call for improved
L45@P1: surveillance of the U.S. Treasury market to better separate its safety attributes from potential
L46@P1: vulnerabilities.
